title: How To Handle An Out-Of-Control Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the rare but severe case of a student who seems untouchable—disrespectful, disruptive, and unmoved by time-out, home consequences, or administrative intervention. His proposed strategy is to strengthen accountability dramatically: formally telling the student, with parents and the principal informed, that they are no longer a full participating member of the class until they prove otherwise. This means excluding them from group work, games, and active recess participation while still requiring academic work and observation-only status. He frames this not as punishment for its own sake but as the strongest lever left to widen the gap between what the student is missing and what they could have, arguing the strategy is reserved only for extreme cases within an otherwise well-managed classroom.
points: The strategy is reserved specifically for a rare, extremely difficult regular-education student in an otherwise well-managed classroom—not for general use.
It requires first notifying the parent(s) and principal, then informing the student they are no longer a full participating member of the class.
The student loses access to group work, games, and active recess participation, but must still complete all academic work as an observer.
The goal is to widen the contrast between the appeal of full class membership and the emptiness of exclusion until the student chooses to change.
A minimum wait of a couple of days is recommended before considering reinstatement, and only once the student requests it and shows behavioral proof.
quotes: So you have this student who seems determined to ruin your school year.

He is one of those rare students who has gotten a peek behind the curtain and has discovered that no matter what he does, within fifteen minutes or so he’ll be right back out on the playground or in your classroom doing as he wishes.
He knows your hands are tied. He knows you’ve tried everything. He knows he’s got you over a barrel.
You explain that his desk will be set apart until he can prove to you he can behave like a full-fledged, contributing member of the classroom.
Students like this need accountability, desperately. And down deep they know it. Their behavior screams out for it, craves it, pleads for it.
You may very well be the only person in his life in position to make such a heroic and potentially life-changing, life-saving stand.
